primary_citation.popular_name: Search and Seizure — State Floor Above Fourth Amendment

key_holding: The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable seizures and searches may not be violated. Warrants require probable cause, oath or affirmation, and particularity. Prior to Prop. 8 (1982) and Prop. 115 (1990), California courts interpreted this provision more broadly than the Fourth Amendment. Section 24 (as amended by Prop. 115) now constrains criminal-case search-and-seizure rights to the federal floor, but CIVIL cases retain independent state grounds.

amendment_history.event: Prop. 7 (Res.Ch. 90, 1974) — Section 13 added as part of comprehensive Article I revision
Prop. 8 (Victims' Bill of Rights) — began the process of aligning California search-and-seizure with federal standards in criminal cases
Prop. 115 — amended §24 to require criminal-case interpretation consistent with US Constitution, effectively overriding independent state grounds for criminal defendants

doctrinal_note: The §24 lockstep provision applies ONLY to criminal cases. In civil cases — including the steward's §1983 claims, conservatorship challenges, and privacy actions — §13 retains full independent state grounds. This is a critical distinction.
